DAW 8: Your First Session in a Real DAW

Step by step in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, linked to each manual: setup, import, record, automate, bounce.

Everything in the small DAW is in BandLab, Ableton Live and Logic Pro, under other names and in other places. This lesson is a checklist for your first session in one of them, then a small project: bring in the song you made here, and add the things the small DAW can’t do.

Each step links to the page in that program’s own manual (BandLab Help Center, the Ableton Live 12 Reference Manual, the Logic Pro 12.3 User Guide). Menus move between versions: if a step doesn’t match what you see, the linked page is the one to trust.

Before you start

  • Headphones, wired. Bluetooth headphones add a delay you can hear: BandLab’s help puts wired at about 5–10 ms and Bluetooth anywhere from 34 to 300 ms (BandLab: what is latency?).
  • Your files from DAW 7: mini-daw.mid (the notes) and, if you like, mini-daw.wav (the mix, to compare with).
  • A name for the project, and a folder to keep it in.

The checklist

  • BandLab
  • Ableton Live
  • Logic Pro

BandLab runs in the browser (and as a phone app). Projects are saved to your BandLab account, so there is no folder to choose. Keyboard shortcuts work only in the web Studio (shortcuts).

  1. Open the Studio and start a new project (Getting started with the Studio).
  2. Tempo and metronome. Open the arrow next to the metronome in the transport bar: tempo, click sound, click volume and a count-in for recording. M turns the click on and off (Using the metronome).
  3. Bring in your MIDI file. The web Studio imports MIDI files as well as audio (WAV, MP3 and others) (supported formats). Then pick an instrument for each track; give the drum track a drum kit.
  4. Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Double-click a MIDI region to edit its notes; select notes and quantize (right-click → Quantize, or Q) (Editing MIDI regions). Slice a region at the playhead with S, duplicate with Alt/Option-drag (Slicing and merging, Duplicating and extending).
  5. Record audio. Add a Voice/Audio track, put your headphones on, and press R to record (R again stops). Hearing yourself (monitoring) is offered on Voice/Audio, Guitar and Bass tracks (Studio FAQ).
  6. Fix the latency if your take lands late: BandLab has an automatic latency test; on iPhone and iPad it corrects itself (Fixing latency).
  7. One effect, one automation move. Add an effect to the voice track (an EQ, a limiter), then switch on automation in the timeline and draw points so the voice comes up in the chorus (BandLab blog: the Mix Editor).
  8. Download the mix. Project → Download → Mixdown As, then choose the format; single tracks can be downloaded as audio or MIDI (Downloading tracks, Exporting MIDI).

Live has two views: Arrangement (the timeline, as in these lessons) and Session (a grid of clips to launch). Tab switches. Work in Arrangement for this project. All shortcuts: Live keyboard shortcuts.

  1. Set up audio. Live → Settings (Mac) or Options → Settings (Windows), Cmd/Ctrl+, → Audio: choose the driver and the input and output device (Audio settings; on Windows an ASIO driver is recommended; setting up an audio interface). The same page shows the buffer size and the overall latency.
  2. Save the Set straight away (File → Save Live Set As). Live makes a Project folder for it; when you finish, File → Collect All and Save copies every sound the Set uses into that folder (saving Sets, collecting files).
  3. Tempo and metronome: the tempo box and the metronome switch in the Control Bar (O); the count-in is in the menu next to the metronome (metronome settings, count-in).
  4. Bring in your MIDI file: drag it from Live’s browser into the Arrangement, or Create → Import MIDI File (MIDI files). Each track arrives as a MIDI clip with no sound: drop an instrument on each, and a Drum Rack kit on the drum track.
  5. Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Draw mode B; quantize Cmd/Ctrl+U; split Cmd/Ctrl+E; duplicate Cmd/Ctrl+D; loop the selection Cmd/Ctrl+L (splitting clips, the Arrangement loop).
  6. Record audio. Insert an audio track (Create → Insert Audio Track), choose its input, arm it, and press the Arrangement Record button (F9) (choosing an input, arming tracks). An armed track is monitored by default (Auto); with speakers, set its monitor to Off (monitoring).
  7. Fix the latency if your take lands late: Driver Error Compensation in Settings → Audio. It only applies to tracks with the monitor set to Off (Driver Error Compensation FAQ).
  8. One effect, one automation move. Drag an audio effect onto the voice track. Press A to show automation, pick the track’s volume, and draw (or click) points so the voice comes up in the chorus (drawing and editing automation).
  9. Export. File → Export Audio/Video (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+R) for the mix; File → Export MIDI Clip for the notes of one clip (exporting audio, exporting MIDI).

Mac only. The user guide is for Logic Pro 12.3 (the version menu on each page goes back to older ones).

  1. Set up audio. Logic Pro → Settings → Audio → Devices: the input and output device, and the I/O Buffer Size. Small for recording (less delay), large for mixing (more plug-ins); clicks and crackles mean it’s too small (Audio Devices settings, managing monitoring latency).
  2. New project. File → New from Template (Cmd+N), New Project; open Details to set the tempo, key, time signature and the input and output device (Create projects). Every Cmd+S keeps a backup; File → Revert to goes back to one (alternatives and backups).
  3. Metronome: K; count-in Shift+K; Control-click the metronome button to choose when it clicks (Use the metronome). Cycle: C (the cycle area).
  4. Bring in your MIDI file: File → Import → MIDI File (it lands at the playhead), or drag it from the Finder into the Tracks area (Standard MIDI files). Choose a patch for each track.
  5. Edit like DAW 3 and 4. Double-click a region for the Piano Roll; quantize with the Time Quantize menu and its Strength slider (it can always be undone) (quantize note timing). Edit → Split → Regions at Playhead (split regions), Edit → Repeat (repeat regions). Mixer: X. The band’s role is played by Session Players (Drummer, Bass Player, Keyboard Player) (Session Players); drum steps by the Step Sequencer (overview).
  6. Record audio. Add Tracks (Option+Cmd+N) → Audio → Mic or Line, choose the Audio Input (Create tracks). Select the track, headphones on, R records, Space stops (record from a microphone). The guide itself says to use headphones when the metronome is on, so the click isn’t recorded.
  7. Monitoring: the I button on the track header; it always adds some delay (input monitoring). Record → Low Latency Mode keeps it small (managing monitoring latency).
  8. One effect, one automation move. Add a plug-in in an Audio FX slot (plug-ins). Press A to show automation, choose Volume, and click to add points (show automation, add points).
  9. Bounce. File → Bounce → Project or Section; move the End a little past the last region so reverb tails aren’t cut off (bounce a project). Notes out: File → Export → Selection as MIDI File.

The project

Rebuild your small-DAW song, then do three things it couldn’t:

  1. Same song, new sounds. Import mini-daw.mid, choose instruments, match the tempo. Play both mixes: what changed?
  2. Record one real part with a microphone, in headphones, to the click (DAW 6). Record it three times and keep the best. Real DAWs keep every pass (takes) and let you build one from the best bits (comping): Logic, Ableton.
  3. Add one effect and one automation move. Reverb on the voice, the chorus louder than the verse.
  4. Bounce it, listen on earbuds and on a phone speaker, and fix the loudest problem (Recording 7: Mixing).

What you’ll meet that wasn’t here

  • A loop and sound library: BandLab’s Sounds, Live’s browser, Logic’s Apple Loops. Fast to start with; remember everyone else has them too.
  • Plug-ins: EQ, compressors, reverb, delay, amp models, synths. The sound-design lessons taught what they do; now it’s only finding them.
  • Automation: any knob can move by itself through the song.
  • Generated parts: Logic’s Session Players and BandLab’s SongStarter do what the band does in DAW 4.
  • Clip launching: Live’s Session View and Logic’s Live Loops, for trying ideas live before arranging them.

When something goes wrong

What happens Likely cause Fix
No sound at all The wrong output device The audio settings (step 1)
Clicks and crackles Buffer too small for the computer Raise the buffer size one step
Hearing yourself late Monitoring latency, Bluetooth Wired headphones, smaller buffer, Low Latency Mode, or monitoring off
Takes land late on the grid Recording latency The latency fix (BandLab test, Live’s Driver Error Compensation)
A howl Monitoring through speakers Headphones, or monitoring off
Click or band in the vocal Bleed Headphones (DAW 6)
The bounce crackles or sounds squashed The master clipped Pull the master down (DAW 5)
